headline: Boston plans five free Link Bus routes, including new Mattapan and Roxbury shuttles
dek: The city expects to launch neighborhood shuttle services in early 2027 with about $11.5 million in federal funding, but routes and stops in Mattapan and Roxbury have not been finalized.
body: Boston plans to launch five free, publicly accessible Link Bus services as soon as early 2027, including new fixed-route shuttles for Mattapan and Roxbury that are intended to connect residential areas with MBTA stations, commercial districts and other daily destinations. The [City of Boston](https://www.boston.gov/news/city-boston-prepares-launch-five-free-bus-routes-across-city) announced the program after the city’s Economic Development and Industrial Corporation authorized the funding arrangement in September.

The program is designed around the transportation problem often called the first mile or last mile: a transit stop may be nearby on a map but still difficult to reach from a home, workplace, school or medical appointment. The city says the Link vehicles will run on established neighborhood routes and will not charge riders. That makes the service different from a one-time event shuttle and positions it as a connector to the broader regional network rather than a replacement for MBTA bus or rail service.

Two of the five services will serve Mattapan and Roxbury. The other grant-supported services will cover Allston-Brighton, Charlestown and the Lower Mystic area, and the South Boston Waterfront, according to the city. Some of those services will be operated with transportation management associations, while Boston plans to competitively procure operators for the Mattapan and Roxbury fixed routes.

The funding comes through the Federal Highway Administration’s Congestion Relief Program and is being administered through the Massachusetts Department of Transportation. Boston says the Link Bus portion is approximately $11.5 million and will support three years of shuttle operations. It is part of a larger $21.6 million LINKUP Greater Boston award that also includes about $10 million for expanding Bluebikes and access to e-bikes.

The city’s public notice for the [Sept. 17 EDIC meeting](https://content.boston.gov/public-notices/16604581) listed authorization of a pass-through contract with MassDOT for up to $11,448,556. The notice identified Allston-Brighton, Charlestown, Mattapan, Roxbury and the Seaport as the service areas. The later announcement says that approval allows contracting, community engagement, service planning and launch preparation to move forward.

For Mattapan and Roxbury residents, the most important details are still unsettled. The city has not chosen the operators, and routes, stops, schedules and service models have not been finalized. [WBUR’s report](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/12/link-shuttle-bus-boston-mattapan-roxbury-mbta), originally published by the Dorchester Reporter, said the lines could connect neighborhoods with Blue Hill Avenue and Mattapan Square station, but described those connections as likely rather than final.

Boston says it will work with residents, businesses, elected officials and community organizations to identify the destinations that would benefit most. That process will determine whether the service closes a meaningful access gap or simply duplicates existing routes. It also gives neighborhoods a chance to weigh in before the city locks in stops and operating patterns.

The Link program builds on Boston’s existing support for fare-free MBTA Routes 23, 28 and 29, which the city says will remain free through the end of 2026. The new shuttles are aimed at a different connection problem: helping people reach transit and local destinations in areas where a direct or convenient link is missing. Boston says it will evaluate ridership and demand during the three-year grant period while looking for ways to sustain the services after that funding ends.
author: NorthEast News Desk
